name: The Hash Table
statement: Store key-value pairs so lookups take constant time on average, using a hash function to pick a slot.
statementAccent: using a hash function to pick a slot
meaning: A hash table, also called a hash map, is a data structure that implements an associative array, or dictionary, mapping keys to values. It uses a hash function to compute, from a key, an index, called a hash code, into an array of buckets or slots, from which the desired value can be found. Because the hash function turns a key directly into a location, the hash table can, on average, find, insert, or delete an entry in constant time, order one, independent of the number of elements stored, which is what makes it one of the most heavily used data structures in computing. This average performance holds when the table is well dimensioned; in the worst case, when many keys collide into the same slot, operations can degrade to order n. Collisions, in which different keys hash to the same index, are inevitable whenever there are more possible keys than slots, and hash tables handle them by collision-resolution schemes, chiefly separate chaining, where each bucket holds a linked list of entries, and open addressing, where the table probes for the next free slot using strategies such as linear probing, quadratic probing, or double hashing. The load factor, the ratio of stored entries to buckets, governs performance, which degrades as it rises, so tables are resized and rehashed once the load factor passes a threshold. A good hash function distributes keys uniformly to minimize collisions. Hash tables date to the 1950s, with an early use by Hans Peter Luhn at IBM in 1953, and they underlie the dictionaries, maps, and sets of essentially every programming language.
mechanism: A hash table stores associations between keys and values in an array, using a hash function to convert each key into an array index so that the value can be reached directly rather than by searching. To insert a key-value pair, the hash function maps the key to a bucket index, and the pair is placed there; to look up or delete, the same function recomputes the index and the bucket is examined. Because the hash function does the locating in constant time and the array access is constant time, the average cost of these operations is order one, independent of how many entries the table holds, which is the source of the hash table's speed. The complication is collisions: since the space of possible keys is typically far larger than the number of slots, by the pigeonhole principle different keys must sometimes hash to the same index, and a good hash table must resolve these. Separate chaining stores, at each bucket, a linked list, or other secondary structure, of all entries that hashed there, so a collision simply appends to the list. Open addressing keeps all entries in the array itself and, on collision, probes a deterministic sequence of alternative slots, linear probing stepping one at a time, quadratic probing stepping by growing amounts, and double hashing using a second hash function to set the step. Either way, performance depends on the load factor, the fraction of the table that is occupied: as it approaches one, chains lengthen and probes multiply, so implementations resize the array, typically doubling it, and rehash all entries once the load factor exceeds a threshold, keeping average operations fast. The quality of the hash function is crucial, since one that clusters keys causes frequent collisions and destroys the constant-time guarantee.

examples.text: The hash function turns a key into an array index, letting the value be found without searching.
Colliding keys are stored in a per-bucket linked list, or probed to the next free slot in the array.
When occupancy passes a threshold, the table is enlarged and rehashed to keep operations fast.

variants.name: Open addressing

whyItMatters: The hash table is one of the most important and pervasive data structures in all of computing, the default way to store and retrieve data by key, and it does quiet, essential work almost everywhere software runs. Its central virtue is speed: by turning a key into an array index through a hash function, it achieves average constant-time insertion, lookup, and deletion, so operations that would be slow with a list or even a balanced tree become effectively instantaneous, no matter how many items are stored. This makes hash tables the natural implementation of the dictionary, map, and set types built into nearly every programming language, from Python's dict and Java's HashMap to C++'s unordered_map, and they underlie database indexing, in-memory caches, symbol tables in compilers and interpreters, deduplication, and countless other tasks. The hash table also embodies a deep and elegant idea, that clever hashing can trade a small, controlled probability of collision for enormous gains in speed, and its study introduces collisions, load factors, and the craft of designing good hash functions, all central themes in algorithms. Reaching back to work by Hans Peter Luhn at IBM in 1953, the hash table has been fundamental for seven decades. As the structure that stores key-value pairs for constant-time access, the hash table is a cornerstone of computer science.

working.text: apply the hash function to compute an array index, or bucket, for the key.
resolve keys that share a bucket by chaining them in a list or probing for a free slot.
grow and rehash the table when the load factor rises, keeping average operations constant time.

limits: The hash table is fast but its guarantees are average-case and conditional, and several points reward care. Its celebrated constant-time performance is an average, holding when the hash function distributes keys well and the load factor is controlled; in the worst case, when many keys collide, operations degrade to order n, and adversarially chosen keys can deliberately provoke this, a real security concern that randomized hashing mitigates. A hash table does not keep its keys in sorted order, so it cannot efficiently support ordered operations like range queries or finding the next-largest key, for which balanced search trees or B-trees are used instead. Performance depends heavily on the hash function and the load factor, and resizing, though amortized cheap, causes occasional expensive rehashing pauses. Memory overhead is real, since tables keep spare capacity to stay below the load-factor threshold. Some historical and technical details reward care: hashing dates to the 1950s, with Hans Peter Luhn's 1953 IBM work an early example, and the two main collision-resolution families, separate chaining and open addressing, behave differently and should not be conflated. So the hash table robustly gives constant-time key access on average, understood as a structure whose speed depends on good hashing and load management and which sacrifices order for speed.
misreadings: The hash table's constant time is an average, not a guarantee; heavy collisions or adversarial keys can degrade it to order n. It does not keep keys ordered, so it cannot do range queries efficiently. And its speed depends on the hash function and load factor, not magic, so treating hash-table operations as worst-case constant, as order-preserving, or as independent of hashing quality, misreads it.
origin: The associative-array data structure, dating to the 1950s with Hans Peter Luhn's 1953 IBM work, that maps keys to values via a hash function for average constant-time access.
